artists.biography:
The Wonder Stuff are a British alternative rock band, originally based in Stourbridge, West Midlands, in the Black Country, England.

The original line-up was Miles Hunt vocals, guitar (whose uncle Bill Hunt was keyboard player with ELO and Wizzard), Malcolm Treece guitar, vocals, Rob "The Bass Thing" Jones (died July 1993) and Martin Gilks, drums (died April 2006). The group originated from an earlier collaboration with group members of Pop Will Eat Itself, called 'From Eden', which had Miles Hunt on the drums.
 
The Wonder Stuff were formed on 19 March 1986. They entered the studio in September that year to record a self-financed first EP A Wonderful Day. After signing with Polydor Records for Â£80,000 in 1987, the group released a series of singles including "Unbearable", "Give Give Give, Me More More More", "A Wish Away" and "It's Yer Money I'm After Baby" (their first Top 40 entry) which were featured on their debut album The Eight Legged Groove Machine in August 1988 (UK #18). The group then embarked on their first headlining nineteen date 'Groovers On Manoeuvres' UK tour. They released "Who Wants To Be The Disco King?" in March 1989, and appeared at Reading and Glastonbury festivals, and tours of Europe and the United States.

perplexity.description:
Never Loved Elvis" is the third studio album by British rock band The Wonder Stuff, originally released in 1991 on Polydor Records. Musically, the album blends alternative rock with elements of pop and folk, showcasing the band's knack for catchy melodies, witty lyrics, and dynamic arrangements. The record features guest appearances from notable musicians such as Kirsty MacColl and Linda McRae, adding depth and variety to its sound. Tracks like "Welcome to the Cheap Seats" and "The Size of a Cow" highlight the band's ability to merge energetic guitar-driven rock with introspective songwriting.

Within The Wonder Stuff's discography, "Never Loved Elvis" stands as a pivotal release, marking a shift toward a more polished and diverse sonic palette compared to their earlier, rawer work. The album was well-received by critics for its songcraft and lyrical intelligence, and it achieved commercial success, reaching high positions on the UK Albums Chart. It remains a significant entry in the band's catalog, often cited as one of their most accomplished works and a standout example of early 1990s British rock.
